Quantile Function of the Modified Half-Normal Distribution

Source: R/qmhn.R
qmhn.Rd

Computes the quantile (inverse cumulative) function of the Modified Half-Normal (MHN) distribution with parameters alpha, beta, and gamma.

Usage

qmhn(p, alpha = 1, beta = 1, gamma = 0, lower.tail = TRUE, log.p = FALSE)

Arguments

p

Numeric vector of probabilities.

alpha

Shape parameter (\(\alpha > 0\)). Scalar or numeric vector. Default: 1.

beta

Rate-type parameter (\(\beta > 0\)), the coefficient of the Gaussian tail \(\exp(-\beta x^2)\); larger values pull mass toward zero. Scalar or numeric vector. Default: 1.

gamma

Tilt parameter (\(\gamma \in R\)), the coefficient of the exponential tilt \(\exp(\gamma x)\). Scalar or numeric vector. Default: 0.

lower.tail

Logical; if TRUE (default), probabilities are \(P(X \le x)\), otherwise \(P(X > x)\), \(x\) being the quantile returned.

log.p

Logical; if TRUE, probabilities are provided on the log scale. Default: FALSE. Both flags are read with as.logical(), so that 1 is TRUE; a value that gives NA is an error.

Value

A numeric vector. The output length equals max(length(p), length(alpha), length(beta), length(gamma)), or 0 if any of them has length zero; each input is recycled to that length following standard R recycling rules. As in qgamma, an element whose parameters lie outside the parameter space (alpha or beta not positive and finite, or gamma not finite) is NaN, with a warning, and an element with an NA or NaN among its inputs is NA or NaN (NA if any of them is NA), without one; the other elements are unaffected. The arguments must be numeric (double, integer or logical): a factor, a character string, a complex number, a list or NULL is an error, as in qnorm. qmhn(0) = 0 and qmhn(1) = Inf. Probabilities outside \([0, 1]\) (log probabilities above 0 when log.p = TRUE) yield NaN, with a warning as in qnorm. If the distribution function cannot be evaluated where the root is sought, a warning is issued and NA is returned for that element. The attributes of p (names, dim, dimnames) are kept when the result has the length of p; a classed p, such as a Date, is taken as its numbers and gives a plain vector. Unlike qnorm, attributes of a longer parameter vector are not carried over.

Details

For the general case, \(q = F^{-1}(p)\) is obtained by a TOMS 748 root-finder applied to the distribution function computed as in pmhn, or for lower.tail = FALSE to the logarithm of its directly computed upper tail. Near 1 that logarithm is about \(-(1 - p)\), and its error, set by the size of the terms it is assembled from (see pmhn), is a relative error in \(1 - p\). Where that could pass \(10^{-9}\), within about \(3 \times 10^{-6}\) of 1 at the least and further out for a large shape, tilt or \(|\log\beta|\), the distribution function is solved for one minus the probability instead, which is exact. Where pmhn takes that distribution function from the series of Sun et al. (2023), which can cost far more than the upper tail (\(\alpha < 1\) with \(|z|\) up to about 830, and \(\alpha \le 100\) with \(|z| \le 20\), \(z = \gamma/\sqrt{\beta}\)), the root of the upper tail is refined instead by Newton steps on the logarithm of the distribution function (taken as in pmhn for the log upper tail). A lower-tail p there is solved on the series itself, and for \(\alpha < 1\) with \(|z|\) from about 100 one quantile can take from a tenth of a second to seconds (about 1 s at \(\alpha = 0.8\), \(z = 829\) and \(p = 0.5\)); where \(1 - p\) is known exactly, lower.tail = FALSE gives the same quantile at once. Within \(10^{-7}\) of 1, where the upper tail may not resolve one minus the probability at all, that root is taken for a probability it does resolve where needed, and the steps start from it. Likewise a lower-tail p close to 1 (within \(10^{-7}\) of 1 at least; see Range), where the distribution function is resolved only to the rounding of 1, is solved on the logarithm of the upper tail for one minus it, which is exact. A lower-tail log.p probability below log(.Machine$double.xmin), about -708.4, whose exponential is no longer a normal double, is solved on the logarithm of the distribution function. The initial bracket is \([s\sqrt{\epsilon},\; s]\) with \(s = E(X) + 8 \sqrt{\mathrm{Var}(X)}\), which scales with the distribution. Its left end is halved (down to the smallest positive double) and its right end doubled (up to the largest double) until it brackets the target probability, each step keeping the bracket a factor of two wide. Where the root-finder does not reach its tolerance on that bracket, as for a tiny lower-tail p with a large \(\alpha\), the equation is solved again for \(\log q\) on the logarithm of the distribution function, and where that fails too, or the bracket lies near the largest double, the bracket is bisected. The root is found to a relative \(2^{-46}\), and where pmhn measures the law from its peak (see there) also to within \(2^{-46}\) of the law's standard deviation, which can be narrower. A quantile below .Machine$double.xmin is resolved to the spacing of the subnormal doubles there, about \(4.9 \times 10^{-324}\), and one below that spacing is returned as 0, as qgamma returns a quantile that underflows; a quantile beyond the largest double is returned as Inf, as qgamma returns one that overflows.

Range. The quantile inverts pmhn, whose range of accuracy it inherits: for \(\alpha \le 10^{15}\), \(|z| \le 10^{15}\) and \(\beta\) in \([10^{-300}, 10^{300}]\) it is the root, to the tolerance above or to the spacing of the doubles near it, whichever is larger, of an equation that resolves the smaller of the two tail probabilities to about \(2 \times 10^{-9}\) of itself or better (see there), which places it within about that many of the law's standard deviations. Next to the origin, where \(F(x)\) is about a multiple of \(x^\alpha\), its relative error is that of the smaller tail probability divided by about \(\alpha\). A lower-tail p close to 1 is solved on the upper tail, as the root of \(P(X > x) = 1 - p\) with \(1 - p\) formed exactly, wherever the error of \(F\) near 1 could pass \(10^{-9}\) of \(1 - p\) and the upper tail resolves it more accurately: \(F\) is resolved there only to the rounding of 1, and for a small shape, where it is close to 1 over most of the range, to the error of the lower tail (see pmhn). At parameters of order one that is so within about \(10^{-5}\) of 1, and farther for a small or large shape, a large tilt or an extreme \(\beta\). Where the law is narrower than the spacing of the doubles (for \(z\) above about \(10^{16}\), or \(\alpha\) above about \(10^{31}\)) its distribution function is a step between two adjacent doubles, and the quantile of every p strictly inside \((0, 1)\) is the one of the two nearer to the true quantile, placed from the exact offset of the law's peak. Where pmhn is NA (see there), so is the quantile, with a warning. Where the log upper tail of pmhn is -Inf in place of a finite value (\(\beta\) and the tilt both close to the largest double, see there), the quantile of a log.p probability beyond that point is the point at which it turns -Inf, without a warning.

At \(\gamma = 0\) and at \(\alpha = 1\) exactly the quantile is computed from the law it reduces to; a shape or a tilt merely close to those values is a different law, and is computed as in the general case:

  • \(\gamma = 0\): \(q = \sqrt{y / \beta}\), where \(P(\alpha/2, y) = p\) for the regularized incomplete gamma function \(P\) (Sun et al. 2023, Lemma 6a); \(y\) is taken from qgamma, or from the leading term of \(P\) where it is below the smallest normal double; for \(\alpha \le 10^6\). Above it \(\gamma = 0\) is solved on the distribution function measured from the peak, as for any other tilt (see pmhn).

  • \(\alpha = 1\): the truncated-normal inverse (Sun et al. 2023, Lemma 6b), by qnorm, refined by one Newton step on the scaled complementary error function where the truncation point 0 lies three or more standard deviations above the mean \(\gamma/(2\beta)\) of the untruncated normal, \(-\gamma/\sqrt{2\beta} \ge 3\), and by Newton's method on that function alone where it lies more than 30 standard deviations above it. Near the truncation point it is solved by Halley's method on a short series, so that the quantile of a small lower-tail probability keeps its relative accuracy. Where \(-\gamma/\sqrt{2\beta}\) overflows the law is Exponential with rate \(|\gamma|\), and its quantile is that one's.

When any of alpha, beta, gamma is a vector, the quantile is evaluated element-wise. The Fox-Wright \(\Psi\) normalizing constant and moments \(E(X)\), \(\mathrm{Var}(X)\) (used to size the root-finder bracket) are computed once for each position of the recycling cycle while that cycle is at most 256 long, and otherwise once for each run of consecutive elements that share the \((\alpha, \beta, \gamma)\) triple.

References

Sun, J., Kong, M., & Pal, S. (2023). The Modified-Half-Normal distribution: Properties and an efficient sampling scheme. Communications in Statistics - Theory and Methods, 52(5), 1591–1613.

See also

dmhn, pmhn, rmhn

Examples

# Basic evaluation
qmhn(c(0.1, 0.5, 0.9), alpha = 2, beta = 1, gamma = 1)
#> [1] 0.4717434 1.0906276 1.8480472

# Round-trip: F(F^-1(p)) ~ p
p <- c(0.05, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 0.95)
all.equal(pmhn(qmhn(p, alpha = 2, beta = 1, gamma = 1),
               alpha = 2, beta = 1, gamma = 1),
          p, tolerance = 1e-6)
#> [1] TRUE

# Tail / log forms
qmhn(0.95, alpha = 2, beta = 1, gamma = 1, lower.tail = FALSE)
#> [1] 0.3394014
qmhn(log(0.05), alpha = 2, beta = 1, gamma = 1, log.p = TRUE)
#> [1] 0.3394014
